columns.description: what one unit of `from_currency` was worth in `to_currency` on `date_day`. Same-currency pairs are present and are exactly 1. An amount is still converted at its own day's rate, never at an averaged one (rule ExchangeRate.convert_per_day).

columns.description: WHICH CHANNEL THE SALE WAS IN — `physical` for a shop you can walk into, `online` for the web shop. Derived on the fact from the store key (`store_key = 999999` is the web shop), so it needs no join and is reachable from every question whatever route it takes. Measured equivalent to `dim_store.location_code = -1` on 2026-10-23, with zero disagreements. The value names are the populations rule Store.channel declares, so the axis has one vocabulary. A FINANCIAL QUESTION THAT NAMES NO CHANNEL COVERS BOTH, by the operator's ruling of 2026-10-18 (rule Store.channel). Before this column that reading was the ABSENCE of a predicate, which no gate could check and no answer could disclose; now it can be grouped, stated and verified.
columns.name: channel

columns.description: true on every web-shop line, false on every shop line, never empty; the same split as `channel`, as true / false. Made by the transform so that rule Order.channel reads its `shops` and `online` options from a column instead of a stored value.
columns.name: is_web_sale

columns.description: THE COUNTRY OF THE SALE — the ISO code of the country this line is trade IN. A shop sale is attributed to the country the SHOP stands in; a web sale to the country the CUSTOMER lives in. Derived on the fact from `channel` and the two keys, so it needs no join and is reachable from every question whatever route the question takes. This is the reading an unqualified country question means (operator ruling 2026-10-25); the store's, the customer's and the site's own country stay askable BY NAME through their own relations. EVERY LINE REACHES A COUNTRY and none carries the `--` sentinel: the sentinel leaves the country axis of a sale entirely, because a web sale is attributed to a person and a person has a real country. The axis PARTITIONS the sales line — the parts sum to the whole, with no leakage and nothing double counted. The figures that prove it are in the ruling, which is their one home; a figure restated here would be a second home that goes stale on the next load. WHY IT IS NOT `dim_customer.country_code` UNDER ANOTHER NAME, though it is row-for-row identical to it here: no physical sale in this warehouse crosses a border, so the two readings AGREE BY ACCIDENT OF THE DATA. They do not mean the same thing — a German tourist buying in Paris is French trade on this column and German trade on the customer's — and the operator refused `default: customer` on 2026-10-22 for exactly that reason.
columns.name: sale_country_code

columns.description: THE CURRENCY THE SALE WAS TRANSACTED IN, and NOT the unit of the amounts on this row. The amounts are USD. Filtering on this and presenting the amounts as if they were in that currency is forbidden by currency.ambiguity.code_is_not_the_unit_of_the_amounts.
columns.name: currency_code

columns.description: THE CURRENCY THE AMOUNTS ON THIS ROW ARE IN — USD on every line, made by the transform. The upstream publishes it and the warehouse confirms it: the source's own exchange rate on each line is the USD-to-line-currency rate. It is the source currency the exchange-rate edge joins on (order__converts_at__exchange_rate), so the join reads a column instead of a constant. Offered to no question on its own; `currency_code` is the currency a sale was transacted in.
columns.name: unit_currency

columns.description: how many units of the product the line sold.
columns.name: quantity

columns.description: the price actually paid for one unit, in USD, after discount. Upstream: `unit_price * (1 - discount/100)`, and measured never above `unit_price`. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`: the price holds for every unit on the line, so it averages as Σ(quantity × net_price) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `net_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_is_per_article), never as a plain mean of line prices. The generator draws a quantity per order row and prices the row per unit (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").
columns.name: net_price

columns.description: what ONE UNIT ON THIS LINE was charged before discount, in USD. Measured against the source: `unit_price = product.Price × f`, where `f` is the same per-line factor used for `unit_cost = product.Cost × f`. From 2024 onward `f = 1.0`, so this is the current list price level for all products sold in that period. `gross_amount` is exactly `quantity * unit_price`. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`: Σ(quantity × unit_price) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `gross_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_terms), never a plain mean of line prices (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").
columns.name: unit_price

columns.description: what one unit cost Contoso, in USD. Upstream it is scaled by the same price factor as `unit_price`, so margin PERCENT is stable within a category while absolute margin moves — a margin-erosion story read off this data is an artefact of the generator. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`; Σ(quantity × unit_cost) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `cost_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_terms), never a plain mean of line costs (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").
columns.name: unit_cost

columns.description: what the customer was actually charged for the line, in USD, after discount: exactly `quantity * net_price`. THE DEFAULT MONEY COLUMN: a question saying revenue or sales without saying net or gross is answered here (rule Order.revenue_means_net). AN UNQUALIFIED PRICE means what the customer paid per article: this column summed and divided by `quantity` summed (operator ruling, 2026-09-30; rule Order.price_is_per_article). When a question says store, shop, product, or placed without naming a competing figure, those words are read on this same sales-line figure.
columns.name: net_amount

columns.description: what the line would have cost at list price, in USD: exactly `quantity * unit_price`, on every line. The figure BEFORE discount.
columns.name: gross_amount

columns.description: what the goods on the line cost Contoso, in USD. Measured: exactly `quantity * unit_cost`.
columns.name: cost_amount

columns.description: the money given away on the line, in USD. Measured: exactly `gross_amount - net_amount`. Upstream the discount is an integer percent from a closed set of 15 steps, 0 to 14.
columns.name: discount_amount

columns.description: the profit on the line, in USD. Measured: exactly `net_amount - cost_amount`, so it is margin on the DISCOUNTED price and not on list.
columns.name: margin_amount

columns.name: valid_to

columns.means: the day after `valid_to`: the half-open end of the validity window, made by the transform. columns.means: THE SITE ITSELF — one row per site, which is what makes this relation the place a question about sites should be answered from. City exists only on the CUSTOMER (`dim_customer.city`), where it is declared personally identifying (`offers.suppressed: DQ-IDENTIFYING-DIM_CUSTOMER-CITY`) and says where a customer lives, not where a shop stands. Surfacing `city` here would bind "which cities" to an INTEGER site code and present codes as city names; unbound, the question fails to bind and the walk says so, which is the correct outcome for a fact this bundle does not hold.
columns.name: location_code

columns.means: the country the site sits in.
columns.name: country_code

columns.means: the name of the country the site sits in, carried here as well as on dim_country.
columns.name: country_name

columns.means: the state, province or region the site sits in.
columns.name: state

columns.means: how many store rows have ever stood at this site. A site re-tenanted has several store rows over time; each is one premises (rule Store.premises_not_place).
columns.name: units_ever_here

columns.means: true on the online placeholder (site code -1, which is not a place), false on every physical site, never empty. Made by the transform so that rule Location.channel reads `physical` as false and `online` as true instead of a stored value; it selects exactly the rows the code test selected. Offered to no question on its own: a question reaches it through the rule.
columns.name: is_online

columns.means: true where a store at this site has closed (at least one of its store rows carries a closing date), false otherwise, never empty. Rule Location.closed reads its `ever` option from it.
columns.name: has_closed_store

columns.means: true where no store at this site trades (every one of its store rows carries a closing date), false otherwise, never empty. Rule Location.closed reads its `now` option from it.
columns.name: is_closed_now

columns.means: the row key: one row per product.
columns.name: product_key

columns.means: the product's code in the source system, unique across all rows.
columns.name: product_code

columns.means: the product's name as a reader would see it.
columns.name: product_name

columns.means: who made the product.
columns.name: manufacturer

columns.means: the brand the product is sold under. Far fewer brands than products, so a question about brands wants the brands and not the products.
columns.name: brand

columns.means: the product's colour.
columns.name: color

columns.means: the product's top-level category.
columns.name: category_name

columns.means: the product's sub-category, one level below `category_name`. Which of the two a question means is a declared ambiguity (ProductCategory.level).
columns.name: sub_category_name

columns.means: the product's weight as the source gives it, in the unit named by `weight_unit` on the same row. NOT OFFERED TO A QUESTION: the column holds weights in several units and is empty for some products, so a sum, an average or a comparison across products would add one unit to another. Bringing every weight to one unit is a transform's job that has not been done (evidence/MODELLING-LOG.md), so no concept serves it.
columns.name: weight

columns.means: the unit the same row's `weight` is in, as the source spells it, blank where the source gives none. NOT OFFERED TO A QUESTION: it exists only to read `weight`, which is not offered until a transform brings every weight to one unit.
columns.name: weight_unit

columns.means:
THE PREMISES — one row per shop per trading period, and the grain every sale is recorded against: `v_contoso5_sales_line.store_key` points here, never at the site. A shop has its own name, floor area, opening date and closing date, because those are properties of premises and not of a place. `999999` is the online outlet.
A PLACE MAY HOLD A SUCCESSION OF PREMISES, which is why this is finer than `location_code` and why the two must never be used interchangeably: summing floor area over premises counts a re-let site once per tenancy, and counting premises answers a different question from counting sites. The `finer_than` ruling below is what says so to a reader.
columns.name: store_key

columns.means: THE SITE code: several store rows can share it over time. The value -1 is the ONLINE PLACEHOLDER and not a place. The transform turns it into `is_online`, which is what rule Store.channel reads (`physical` is false, `online` is true).
columns.name: store_code

columns.means: the store's name as a reader would see it. 'Online store' is the single non-physical outlet. A reading that finds the online channel by MATCHING THIS NAME is right by luck; the channel is `is_online` (rule Store.channel).
columns.name: store_name

columns.means: the country the store trades in. The online store carries '--', the sentinel dim_country names 'Online' and Country.rows excludes — so this column cannot attribute an internet sale to a real country.
columns.name: country_code

columns.means: the state, province or region the store sits in, within its country.
columns.name: state

columns.means: the day the store opened for trade.
columns.name: open_date

columns.means: the day the store closed, or null if it is still trading. THE TRADING-STATE COLUMN: `active` is this being null (Store.trading).
columns.name: close_date

columns.means: why a store stopped trading, where the source said: blank for a trading store, 'Closed' or 'Restructured' for an ended one, null on the online placeholder. Prose from the source, not a closed vocabulary of this bundle's own (rule Store.trading).
columns.name: status_annotation

columns.means: the store's floor area in square metres.
columns.name: square_metres

columns.means: true on the online outlet (its site code is -1), false on every physical shop, never empty. Rule Store.channel reads `physical` as false and `online` as true.
columns.name: is_online

columns.means: true where the store closed for good (`status_annotation` is Closed), false otherwise, never empty. Rule Store.trading reads its `shut` option from it.
columns.name: is_shut

columns.means: true where the store closed and was replaced (`status_annotation` is Restructured), false otherwise, never empty. Rule Store.trading reads its `restructured` option from it.
columns.name: is_restructured

columns.means: the day the rate held.
columns.name: date_day

columns.means: the currency being converted FROM. Every currency appears as a source, so the view is a full matrix of currency pairs and not a USD-only lookup.
columns.name: from_currency

columns.means: the currency being converted TO.
columns.name: to_currency

columns.means: what one unit of `from_currency` was worth in `to_currency` on `date_day`. Same-currency pairs are present and are exactly 1. THE AMOUNTS ON A SALES LINE ARE ALREADY USD, so converting them with this is how a figure silently becomes the wrong currency. ITS AVERAGE IS THE PLAIN MEAN OF THE DAILY RATES, disclosed — one rate per day and ordered pair, the European Central Bank euro reference rate crossed through EUR, a day without a quote carrying the last quoted day's rate, and no traded volume behind any rate to weight it by (evidence in ontology/concepts/ExchangeRate.md, "How the rate averages"). An amount is still converted at its own day's rate, never at an averaged one (rule ExchangeRate.convert_per_day).
columns.name: rate

columns.means: the order this line belongs to; with `line_number` it is this relation's key. An order has one or more lines. The order header is a degenerate dimension here, not a second fact (rule Order.is_the_purchase).
columns.name: order_key

columns.means: which line of the order this is, 0 to 6. One order can hold several products, and the line is the grain of this fact.
columns.name: line_number

columns.means: the day the order was placed. THE PERIOD COLUMN: an unqualified question about when is answered on this and not on `delivery_date` (Order.date).
columns.name: order_date

columns.means: the day the order was delivered. Measured: never before `order_date` and never null. NOT the period a question is answered on unless it says delivery.
columns.name: delivery_date

columns.means: the customer who bought, joining dim_customer. The only route from a sale to a PERSON, and so the only way to attribute internet sales to a country.
columns.name: customer_key

columns.means: the store the sale was rung up at, joining dim_store. Store key `999999` is the single online outlet, and `channel` beside this column states that split on the fact itself — so a question no longer has to reach dim_store to learn which channel a sale was in.
columns.name: store_key

columns.means: the product sold, joining dim_product.
columns.name: product_key

columns.means: WHICH CHANNEL THE SALE WAS IN — `physical` for a shop you can walk into, `online` for the web shop. Derived on the fact from the store key (`store_key = 999999` is the web shop), so it needs no join and is reachable from every question whatever route it takes. Measured equivalent to `dim_store.location_code = -1` on 2026-10-23, with zero disagreements. The value names are the populations rule Store.channel declares, so the axis has one vocabulary. A FINANCIAL QUESTION THAT NAMES NO CHANNEL COVERS BOTH, by the operator's ruling of 2026-10-18 (rule Store.channel). Before this column that reading was the ABSENCE of a predicate, which no gate could check and no answer could disclose; now it can be grouped, stated and verified.
columns.name: channel

columns.means: true on every web-shop line, false on every shop line, never empty; the same split as `channel`, as true / false. Made by the transform so that rule Order.channel reads its `shops` and `online` options from a column instead of a stored value.
columns.name: is_web_sale

columns.means: THE COUNTRY OF THE SALE — the ISO code of the country this line is trade IN. A shop sale is attributed to the country the SHOP stands in; a web sale to the country the CUSTOMER lives in. Derived on the fact from `channel` and the two keys, so it needs no join and is reachable from every question whatever route the question takes. This is the reading an unqualified country question means (operator ruling 2026-10-25); the store's, the customer's and the site's own country stay askable BY NAME through their own relations. EVERY LINE REACHES A COUNTRY and none carries the `--` sentinel: the sentinel leaves the country axis of a sale entirely, because a web sale is attributed to a person and a person has a real country. The axis PARTITIONS the sales line — the parts sum to the whole, with no leakage and nothing double counted. The figures that prove it are in the ruling, which is their one home; a figure restated here would be a second home that goes stale on the next load. WHY IT IS NOT `dim_customer.country_code` UNDER ANOTHER NAME, though it is row-for-row identical to it here: no physical sale in this warehouse crosses a border, so the two readings AGREE BY ACCIDENT OF THE DATA. They do not mean the same thing — a German tourist buying in Paris is French trade on this column and German trade on the customer's — and the operator refused `default: customer` on 2026-10-22 for exactly that reason.
columns.name: sale_country_code

columns.means: THE CURRENCY THE SALE WAS TRANSACTED IN, and NOT the unit of the amounts on this row. The amounts are USD. Filtering on this and presenting the amounts as if they were in that currency is forbidden by currency.ambiguity.code_is_not_the_unit_of_the_amounts.
columns.name: currency_code

columns.means: THE CURRENCY THE AMOUNTS ON THIS ROW ARE IN — USD on every line, made by the transform. The upstream publishes it and the warehouse confirms it: the source's own exchange rate on each line is the USD-to-line-currency rate. It is the source currency the exchange-rate edge joins on (order__converts_at__exchange_rate), so the join reads a column instead of a constant. Offered to no question on its own; `currency_code` is the currency a sale was transacted in.
columns.name: unit_currency

columns.means: how many units of the product the line sold.
columns.name: quantity

columns.means: the price actually paid for one unit, in USD, after discount. Upstream: `unit_price * (1 - discount/100)`, and measured never above `unit_price`. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`: the price holds for every unit on the line, so it averages as Σ(quantity × net_price) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `net_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_is_per_article), never as a plain mean of line prices. The generator draws a quantity per order row and prices the row per unit (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").
columns.name: net_price

columns.means: what ONE UNIT ON THIS LINE was charged before discount, in USD. Measured against the source: `unit_price = product.Price × f`, where `f` is the same per-line factor used for `unit_cost = product.Cost × f`. From 2024 onward `f = 1.0`, so this is the current list price level for all products sold in that period. `gross_amount` is exactly `quantity * unit_price`. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`: Σ(quantity × unit_price) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `gross_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_terms), never a plain mean of line prices (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").
columns.name: unit_price

columns.means: what one unit cost Contoso, in USD. Upstream it is scaled by the same price factor as `unit_price`, so margin PERCENT is stable within a category while absolute margin moves — a margin-erosion story read off this data is an artefact of the generator. ITS AVERAGE IS WEIGHTED BY `quantity`; Σ(quantity × unit_cost) ÷ Σ quantity, which is `cost_amount` ÷ `quantity` (rule Order.price_terms), never a plain mean of line costs (evidence in ontology/concepts/Order.md, "How the per-unit figures average").
columns.name: unit_cost

columns.means: what the customer was actually charged for the line, in USD, after discount: exactly `quantity * net_price`. THE DEFAULT MONEY COLUMN: a question saying revenue or sales without saying net or gross is answered here (rule Order.revenue_means_net). AN UNQUALIFIED PRICE means what the customer paid per article: this column summed and divided by `quantity` summed (operator ruling, 2026-09-30; rule Order.price_is_per_article). When a question says store, shop, product, or placed without naming a competing figure, those words are read on this same sales-line figure.
columns.name: net_amount

columns.means: what the line would have cost at list price, in USD: exactly `quantity * unit_price`, on every line. The figure BEFORE discount.
columns.name: gross_amount

columns.means: what the goods on the line cost Contoso, in USD. Measured: exactly `quantity * unit_cost`.
columns.name: cost_amount

columns.means: the money given away on the line, in USD. Measured: exactly `gross_amount - net_amount`. Upstream the discount is an integer percent from a closed set of 15 steps, 0 to 14.
columns.name: discount_amount

columns.means: the profit on the line, in USD. Measured: exactly `net_amount - cost_amount`, so it is margin on the DISCOUNTED price and not on list.
columns.name: margin_amount
